area: Area IV. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can spot a nose-high or nose-low unusual attitude from the instruments alone, recover to stable level flight in the right order on a full or partial panel, and explain how illusions, startle, automation and inadvertent IMC set up a loss of control.
why: Loss of control in flight is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents. A pilot who reads the panel fast and recovers in the right order turns a scary moment into a non-event.

prereading.what: Unusual attitudes: causes, recognition, nose-high and nose-low recovery, and common errors (analog panel).
prereading.label: IFH 7-26 to 7-29

prereading.what: Glass panel unusual attitude recovery protection, AHRS and ADC failures, standby instruments, autopilot use and errors that lead to unusual attitudes.
prereading.label: IFH 7-55 to 7-59

prereading.what: The inner ear, vestibular and visual illusions, and how to cope with spatial disorientation.
prereading.label: IFH 3-4 to 3-9

prereading.what: Upset definition, causal factors, spatial disorientation, surprise and startle, upset prevention and recovery training, and common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 5, 5-1 to 5-7

prereading.what: Spiral dive recovery in five steps and its common errors.
prereading.label: AFH 5-26 to 5-27

prereading.what: Inadvertent VFR flight into IMC: recognition, keeping control, gentle maneuvers and the transition back to visual flight.
prereading.label: AFH 18-17 to 18-22

prereading.what: Analog instrument failure, vacuum failure and pitot-static failure.
prereading.label: IFH 11-7 to 11-8

warmup: You look up from the GPS and the airspeed is climbing fast, the altimeter is unwinding and you feel perfectly level. Which do you believe, and what do you touch first?

key_terms.def: An airplane attitude not normally required for instrument flight, usually unexpected.
Unintended flight beyond 25° nose up, 10° nose down, 45° bank, or at speeds wrong for the conditions.
Any big unintended departure from the intended flightpath. Leading cause of fatal GA accidents.
Your senses disagree with the airplane's real attitude. Can be recognized, unrecognized or incapacitating.
In a long turn you feel level and see altitude loss, so you pull back and tighten the spiral.
Rapid acceleration feels like nose-up, so the pilot may push into a dive.
An automatic reflex (muscle jerk, racing heart) to a sudden, intense event you did not expect.
Flying without the attitude and heading indicators, using airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator.
A small forward push back toward about +1 G before rolling wings level in a nose-low spiral.
Control and power inputs sized to the size and rate of the upset, so you don't overstress the airplane.

body.p: An unusual attitude is an airplane attitude not normally required for instrument flight. Except in training, it is never intentional, so it is usually a surprise [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
When you find one, the problem is not how you got there. The problem is what the airplane is doing right now and how to get back to straight-and-level flight as fast as possible [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
The AFH uses a newer word, **upset**: an event that unintentionally goes beyond the limits normally seen in flight or training [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

head: Upset parameter
Limit
rows: Inside those limits, but at a speed wrong for the conditions [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]

body.p: An upset includes stalls and overspeeds, has defined limits, and centers on surprise. A training attitude of 30° bank and 15° nose up is an unusual attitude, but not an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

callout.text: In unusual attitude training you are often told to close your eyes while the attitude is set up, so the surprise disappears [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Real upsets come with startle. Train for both.

check.q: You are in a 50° bank with the nose 5° up. Is that an upset by the AFH definition?
check.a: Yes. Any bank greater than 45° meets the upset definition [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

chunks.title: How airplanes get there: causes and prevention

body.p: The IFH lists the usual causes: turbulence, disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, being busy with flight deck duties, a careless cross-check, misreading instruments, and weak aircraft control skills [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

head: Factor (AFH)
Examples
Prevention
rows: Turbulence, mountain waves, wind shear, thunderstorms, wake turbulence, icing [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
Know where these hide. In a thunderstorm, hold a level attitude and let airspeed and altitude vary [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]
Asymmetric flaps, binding controls, runaway trim, autoflight malfunction [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
Know systems and POH procedures. Stay sharp on partial panel [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
VMC into IMC, diverted attention, task saturation, sensory overload, spatial disorientation [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Fly the airplane first, keep the cross-check going, manage workload
Stalls are part of the upset family [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
Watch AOA cues: buffet, loss of roll authority, a descent you can't stop [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]

body.p: **Trim and a tidy flight deck are prevention.** An airplane not trimmed for level flight can turn a short distraction into an emergency if you stop cross-checking [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. A disorganized flight deck does the same: hunting for charts and logs pulls your eyes off the instruments [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
**Physiological factors.** Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia make spatial disorientation more likely [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

callout.text: A fatigued pilot in IMC at night with a vacuum pump failure, or one who forgets pitot heat, can lose control because of long, unpracticed partial panel flight [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

check.q: Name two habits that keep a short distraction from becoming an unusual attitude.
check.a: Keep the airplane trimmed for level flight [[23:219|IFH 7-58]] and keep the flight deck organized so you never stop the cross-check [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: Your inner ear senses motion with fluid in three canals. In a steady turn, after about 15 to 20 seconds the fluid catches up and you feel no turn at all [[23:71|IFH 3-4]] [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. When you roll out, you feel a turn the other way and may roll back into the original turn [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

head: Illusion
Cause
What the disoriented pilot does
rows: A bank entered too slowly to sense, then corrected abruptly [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Rolls back into the original bank, or leans in the seat [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Abrupt head movement in a long constant-rate turn [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Feels rotation on a different axis; maneuvers into a dangerous attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Long coordinated turn feels level; altitude loss is seen [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Pulls back, tightening the spiral and losing more altitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Rapid acceleration feels nose-up; rapid deceleration feels nose-down [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Pushes into a dive, or pulls into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Abrupt change from climb to level flight [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Feels tumbling backward; pushes abruptly nose-low [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Updraft feels like a climb, so pushes nose-low; downdraft the opposite [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Sloping clouds, ground lights and stars; a stared-at light seems to move [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Lines up with the wrong reference and loses control [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]

body.p: Accident data from 2008 to 2013 show nearly 200 spatial disorientation accidents, more than 70% fatal. Disorientation can be recognized, unrecognized (you don't know it's happening) or incapacitating (you can't recover) [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

bullets: Keep head movement small in your scan. If you drop something, pick it up with little head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
Get a good weather briefing and don't continue into bad weather or darkness unless you are proficient on instruments [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].
Most important: become proficient on instruments, trust them, and disregard your sensations [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

callout.text: Feel level but see the altimeter unwinding? Think graveyard spiral. Level the wings on the instruments before you pull.

check.q: During a long turn in IMC you reach back for a chart. Which illusion are you inviting?
check.a: The Coriolis illusion, from a head movement in a different plane during a prolonged turn [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

body.p: **Surprise** is an unexpected event that upsets your thinking. **Startle** is an automatic reflex (muscle jerk, racing heart, higher blood pressure) to a sudden, intense event [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

An untrained pilot reacts by instinct, not thought, with abrupt muscle effort. That is hazardous in turbulence, at high speed, or near the ground [[24:109|AFH 5-4]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The instinct in a nose-down attitude is to pull back on the elevator [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

head: Threat
What happens
Counter
rows: Requirements exceed your capability; the safety margin is gone [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Shed tasks: fly first, then navigate and talk
Many warnings at once, or an expected warning that never comes [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Cross-check to confirm what is real, missing or invalid [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Setting avionics or chasing a malfunction while hand flying [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
Trim, then do one short task at a time
High risk in a sudden developing upset [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]
Inputs in proportion to the size and rate of the upset [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]

body.p: Scenario-based training with realistic distractions, enough to raise your stress, helps protect you from a disabling startle reaction [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. These skills are perishable and need regular practice [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

callout.text: Say it out loud when something looks wrong: "Unusual attitude, nose low, power." Naming it turns a reflex into a procedure.

check.q: What kind of training best protects you from a startle response in a real upset?
check.a: Scenario-based training with realistic distractions that raise stress, not just eyes-closed maneuvers [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

chunks.title: Recognize and assess: read the whole panel

body.p: Rule: any time an instrument moves at a rate, or shows a value, that does not fit the maneuver you are flying, assume an unusual attitude. Speed up the cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or an instrument failure [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

head: Instrument
Nose-high
Nose-low
rows: Nose above the horizon, except in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]

body.p: **Can you trust the attitude indicator?** A spillable type may have passed its limits or failed. A nonspillable type that works can still be off by up to 5° in pitch and bank and is hard to read in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Older gyros tumbled past about 60° of pitch or 100° of roll [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

callout.text: Use the POH/AFM recovery procedure if there is one. If not, start the recovery by reference to the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
Airspeed is the deciding clue. Slowing = nose high. Speeding up = nose low.

check.q: Airspeed is increasing, the altimeter is unwinding and the turn coordinator shows a left turn. What attitude?
check.a: Nose-low, diving left turn, like IFH Figure 7-40 [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: nose-high recovery

body.p: If airspeed is decreasing or below what you want, you are nose-high and heading toward a stall. Make these inputs almost at the same time, but in this order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]:

bullets: 1. **Power:** increase power, in proportion to how fast you are slowing [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
2. **Pitch:** apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
3. **Bank:** level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder. Level the miniature aircraft and center the ball [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
4. **Confirm level pitch:** the airspeed and altimeter needles reverse and then stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
5. **Confirm straight, coordinated flight:** level miniature aircraft and a centered ball on the turn coordinator [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
6. **Return:** if you started at an assigned altitude (from your instructor or ATC), climb or descend back to it after you are stable [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

body.p: Why power first? In a nose-high attitude your energy is draining away. Power slows the loss, and lowering the nose reduces the angle of attack. AFH stall recovery agrees: reducing AOA is crucial, and adding power reduces altitude loss but does not by itself fix a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

callout.text: Don't roll first and pull. Rolling or pulling while the wing is near the critical angle of attack invites a stall. In the AFH stall recovery, the nose comes down before the wings are rolled level [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
On a glass PFD, red chevrons point back to the horizon. Pointing down means nose-high: lower the nose toward them [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

check.q: Without using the attitude indicator, how do you know the nose has reached level pitch?
check.a: The airspeed and altimeter needles reverse direction and stabilize [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: nose-low recovery and the spiral dive

body.p: If airspeed is increasing or above what you want, you are nose-low. In initial training, recover "by the numbers" in this order. With skill, the inputs blend together [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]:

bullets: 1. **Power:** reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and altitude loss [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
2. **Bank:** level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, using the turn coordinator. Keep the ball centered; slips and skids make disorientation worse [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
3. **Pitch:** raise the nose to level with smooth back elevator pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

4. **Cross-check for overcontrol:** the first control pressures may be large. When the airspeed and altimeter needles slow, you are nearing level; when they stop and reverse, you are passing through level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
5. **Add the attitude indicator back** into the cross-check once the airspeed, altimeter and turn coordinator stabilize [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
6. **Return** to the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

callout.text: The instinct in a nose-down attitude is to pull back [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. With the wings banked, back pressure only steepens the bank and stresses the airplane. Reduce bank first, then raise the nose [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

body.p: **The spiral dive** is a nose-low upset: a tight, steep, descending turn where airspeed and G-load build fast. It usually starts in inadvertent IMC when the pilot follows body sensations. Often the only clue is the sound of rising speed [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The AFH gives five steps:

head: Step
Action
Why
rows: Some forward elevator to about +1 G ("unload")
Lowers AOA and G-load, slows the turn, prevents a rolling pullout [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Gently raise the nose to level
Speed may be at or past VNE; slow, gentle inputs prevent structural failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Climb power once airspeed reaches VY
Climb back to a safe altitude [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]

callout.text: Nose high: Power up, Push, Roll. Nose low: Power down, Roll, then gently Pull.

check.q: Why does the AFH want a small push before you roll out of a spiral dive?
check.a: It unloads the wing to about +1 G, lowering AOA and G-load and avoiding a rolling pullout that can exceed the design limit [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

chunks.title: Partial panel and glass panel failures

body.p: **Spotting the failure.** A warning flag, or an attitude indicator that disagrees with the other instruments, usually means a failure. Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI right away. Then fly with what still works [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Covering failed instruments can help, then tell ATC and declare an emergency if needed [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

A failing vacuum pump lets the gyros slow and wander. If they drive the autopilot or flight director, those can move wrongly too. In Figure 11-8 the airplane is actually level at 2,000 ft MSL, not turning left. Miss the failure flags and you can turn a harmless failure into an unusual attitude that needs a partial panel recovery [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so watch the vacuum gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

**Partial panel recovery** uses the same steps with the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The altimeter becomes your primary pitch instrument. Avoid abrupt yoke inputs: overcontrolling swings you from nose-high to nose-low and back [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. To fix an altitude error, first stop the needle with a smooth input, then change pitch to go back [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

**Glass panels.** The PFD keeps some sky and some ground in view at all times, so you always know the quickest way back to the horizon [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]. The white line is the horizon; the blue-brown break is only a reference [[23:216|IFH 7-55]].

head: IFH example PFD protection
Triggers
rows: Appear approaching 30° nose-up; declutter until pitch is below 25° [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Appear past 15° nose-down; declutter at 20° nose-down [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Past 60°, the roll index extends to show the shortest way to wings level; declutter at 65° [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Show airspeed and altitude 6 seconds ahead [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]

callout.text: If the AHRS fails, all unusual attitude protection is gone, along with attitude and heading on the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With AHRS and air data both failed, the IFH example airplane has only the standby airspeed, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass, and no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

check.q: Your attitude indicator shows a left bank, but the turn coordinator is level and the VSI and altimeter are steady. What do you suspect and do?
check.a: A failed attitude indicator (for example, vacuum failure). Cross-check, fly partial panel with the instruments that agree, cover the bad one and tell ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

chunks.title: Automation: autopilot as tool and trap

body.p: **As a tool.** The autopilot reduces workload and gives you more time to monitor. Using it also lowers the chance of entering an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Flying IMC without an autopilot raises workload, and the RMH lists it as an aircraft hazard to weigh [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

In the IFH example glass airplane, the autopilot has its own turn coordinator behind the MFD. Its roll mode, a wing leveler, stays available unless that turn coordinator fails. With AHRS and air data both failed, the manufacturer recommends turning on that wing leveler [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. After an AHRS failure, all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold are lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

**As a trap.** Upsets can come from autoflight malfunction or misuse, and automation can hide the cause. Disengaging the autopilot lets you control the airplane directly and may remove the problem [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Failing to monitor, over-relying on, or not knowing the automation can lead to an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

head: Situation
Automation action
rows: Recovering from an upset or stall
Disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot first; manual control is essential [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Failing to disconnect is a common recovery error [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
An autopilot driven by wandering gyros can move the airplane wrongly [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Disengage altitude hold and speed hold; they add maneuvering and stress [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]
Let a working autopilot hold the airplane while you do the head-down task [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]

callout.text: Automation can make you safer, but you must stay proficient at hand flying for when it fails [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

check.q: You enter an upset and the autopilot is still engaged. What is the first step?
check.a: Disconnect it and fly manually. Leaving it on can make control or trim changes you don't notice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Operating envelope: load factor and airspeed limits

body.p: Recovering is not just about getting level. It is getting level without stalling or breaking the airplane. In a level, coordinated turn the load factor is 2 G at 60° of bank and 5.76 G at 80° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The normal category limit load factor is 3.8 to -1.52 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

bullets: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor. A 50-knot airplane stalls at 100 knots at 4 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Below maneuvering speed (VA), the airplane stalls before a damaging load builds. VA does not protect against full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
VNE is set for smooth air only. In rough air, slow to maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
Flaps extended mean lower design G-load limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: **Control input errors.** Size your inputs to the size and rate of the upset, so you don't overstress the airplane, unless ground contact is close [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]. A startled pilot in a spiral who yanks back while rolling level can cause structural damage or failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Bringing the nose up abruptly after a recovery can exceed the critical AOA again and cause a secondary stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.307(c): with a non-crewmember aboard, no intentional maneuver beyond 60° of bank or 30° nose up or down unless everyone wears an approved parachute. Flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

check.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots wings level. You pull 4 G in a hurried pullout. At what airspeed can it stall?
check.a: About 100 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor (√4 = 2) [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

chunks.title: Inadvertent IMC: getting back to VMC

body.p: Continued VFR from VMC into marginal VMC and IMC is a factor in loss-of-control accidents. Losing the natural horizon greatly raises the chance of spatial disorientation [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. A pilot without instrument training, or with rusty skills, loses control in about 10 minutes once forced onto the instruments [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

If you can't keep attitude control by the natural horizon, you are in IMC no matter what the weather report says. Treat it as a genuine emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. The first steps: recognize and accept it, keep control, and get help to get the airplane on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

head: Keep control (AFH)
Limit
rows: The most important, in fact the only, concern at first [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Trim for hands-off level flight; fly the attitude indicator with fingertips [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
No more than 10° of bank; turn a few degrees, level, repeat [[24:368|AFH 18-19]]
No more than one bar width up, then add power [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]
Power in small steps, no more than 500 fpm, no more than one bar width down [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]
Use any autopilot or wing leveler you have [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]

body.p: **Get help early.** You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt the weather. Ask for help then, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Climb if possible for better radio and radar coverage, but an unauthorized climb or descent in IFR conditions in controlled airspace is prohibited except under 14 CFR 91.3(b) [[34:45|AIM 6-3-2]]. If you can't reach ATC, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Controllers can give vectors to a landing site, and 121.5 MHz is widely monitored [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

callout.text: ATC may sound urgent. Don't let that rush you into a maneuver that costs control. It's reasonable to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]. When you break out, take time to get oriented before trying to land, even if it means flying straight and level or circling for a while [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

check.q: A VFR pilot slips into cloud. What bank limit does the AFH give for turning back toward better weather?
check.a: No more than 10° of bank, in small steps if a big heading change is needed [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

body.p: **Collision hazards.** Unusual attitude practice happens under a view-limiting device, so someone else must watch for traffic. Simulated instrument flight requires a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class, with adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. Instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during simulated instrument flight and must guard against it [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

bullets: Pick a safe altitude, an area free of traffic, good weather, and radar traffic advisories. The IFH gives this setup for stall practice, and it fits unusual attitude practice too [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
Recoveries can gain or lose a lot of altitude. Clear above and below, not just ahead.
In real IMC you won't see traffic at all. Reduced in-flight visibility raises the risk of missing conflicting traffic [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14.2]].

body.p: **Distractions and task priority.** Many upsets happen while the pilot is busy with a task that pulls attention away from the instruments [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Fixating on one instrument builds tension on the controls and causes new errors [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Priority is always: fly, then navigate, then communicate.

head: SRM / CRM item
What it looks like
rows: Items for the flight neatly arranged; a messy deck makes you stop cross-checking [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]
State the situation clearly and briefly [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]
Give the controls to the most situationally aware pilot [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]
Tell ATC about failures and declare an emergency before it gets beyond you [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Spot flights that need more risk management before you go [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]

callout.text: With your instructor, say "I have the controls" and "you have the controls" out loud. The AFH calls for standardized interactions so the crew works as a team [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

check.q: Who must be in the other seat when you practice unusual attitudes under a hood?
check.a: A safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate for that category and class, with adequate outside vision [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

body.p: **Unusual attitudes (IFH):**

bullets: Not keeping the airplane trimmed [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
A disorganized flight deck that pulls your eyes off the panel [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
Slow cross-check and fixation: stopping to stare at an odd reading [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
Trying to recover by feel instead of sight [[23:190|IFH 7-29]].
Not practicing basic instrument skills; every basic error gets worse in a recovery [[23:190|IFH 7-29]].

body.p: **Upset recoveries (AFH):**

bullets: Assessing the type of upset wrong [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].
Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].
Not unloading the airplane when needed [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].
Rolling the wrong way [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].
Mismanaging airspeed during the recovery [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].
Spiral dive: not reducing power first, adding power, pulling before the wings are level, or pulling while rolling [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

check.q: In a spiral dive, what is wrong with pulling out while rolling the wings level?
check.a: It is a listed common error. A rolling pullout exceeds the design limit more easily and can cause structural damage [[24:132|AFH 5-27]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-39. Unusual attitude-nose-high.
f1.alt: Analog six-pack under a tilted mountain horizon with three labels: gaining altitude (altimeter climbing), climbing right turn (attitude indicator nose up and banked right, turn coordinator right), and airspeed decreasing (airspeed needle low). The VSI shows a climb.

f2.caption: Figure 7-40. Unusual attitude-nose-low.
f2.alt: Analog six-pack with the horizon tilted the other way and three labels: losing altitude (altimeter unwinding), diving left turn (attitude indicator nose down and banked left, turn coordinator left), and airspeed increasing. The VSI shows a descent.

f3.caption: Figure 7-69. Unusual attitude recovery protection. Note the brown horizon line is visible at the bottom.
f3.alt: Garmin PFD in a steep nose-high attitude: almost all blue sky, two large red chevrons above the airplane symbol pointing down toward the horizon, a thin brown ground strip at the bottom, airspeed 108 knots and altitude 5,900 ft on the tapes.

f4.caption: Figure 11-8. Vacuum failure.
f4.alt: Analog panel with a red failure flag on the attitude indicator, which shows a false left bank, and a red flag on the heading indicator. The turn coordinator is level, the VSI shows zero and the altimeter is steady, showing the airplane is really level.

f5.caption: Figure 5-53. Angle of bank changes load factor in level flight.
f5.alt: Graph of load factor in G (0 to 7) against bank angle (0° to 90°). The red curve stays near 1 G to about 30°, reaches 2 G at 60°, then rises steeply past 6 G near 80°.

f6.caption: Figure 3-7. Graveyard spiral.
f6.alt: Drawing of an airplane descending in a widening red spiral labeled graveyard spiral, a blue corkscrew labeled graveyard spin ending in a crash burst, and a dashed blue level circle labeled correct path.

scenario.title: Night reroute, head down, nose down
scenario.setup: You are single pilot, IFR at 6,000 ft at night in solid IMC with light turbulence, in a steam-gauge airplane with a wing leveler you rarely use. You are tired after a long day. ATC gives you a reroute. You hand fly while you dig for a chart and reprogram the GPS, glancing up now and then. A rising wind noise makes you look up: airspeed is near the yellow arc and climbing, the altimeter reads 5,500 and is unwinding, the turn coordinator shows a left turn and the ball is centered. You feel wings level.

questions.q: What is the airplane doing, and why do you feel level?
questions.a: Nose-low, diving left turn [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. A prolonged coordinated turn stops stimulating the inner ear, so it feels level while altitude drops. That is the setup for a graveyard spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. The sound of rising speed is often the first clue [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

Reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder using the turn coordinator, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure. Cross-check for overcontrol until the needles stop and reverse [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. If it has become a steep spiral, unload to about +1 G before rolling level [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: The airspeed is high. How hard should you pull once the wings are level?
questions.a: Gently. Speed may be near or past VNE, so slow inputs prevent structural failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Size inputs to the upset [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]. VNE is a smooth-air number, and you are in turbulence [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

questions.q: Should you grab the wing leveler during the recovery?
questions.a: Fly the recovery by hand. The AFH says to disconnect a wing leveler or autopilot in a recovery, and failing to is a common error [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. Once stable, a working autopilot cuts workload for the reroute and lowers the chance of another unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

questions.q: You're level again at 5,200 ft, assigned 6,000. What now, and what do you tell ATC?
questions.a: Climb back to the assigned altitude once stable [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Tell ATC what happened and ask for help or time if you need it; an urgency condition starts the moment you are in doubt [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]] [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

questions.q: What set this up, and how do you prevent it next time?
questions.a: Fatigue, diverted attention and a disorganized flight deck [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Trim first, organize charts before you need them, let the autopilot hold the airplane during head-down work, and keep the cross-check going [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

skills.do: The examiner sets up an unusual attitude and has you recover. Identify nose-high or nose-low from the cross-check, then apply pitch, bank, power and configuration in the correct sequence to stabilized level flight (ACS IR.IV.B.S1). The ACS sets no numeric tolerance for this Task; the examiner looks for correct identification, correct order, smooth inputs and a stabilized result.
skills.practice: Have your instructor set up attitudes while your eyes are closed [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Say the type, then fly the IFH order: nose-high is power, push, roll; nose-low is power, roll, raise the nose [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Repeat with the attitude indicator covered, using airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

skills.do: Use SRM or CRM: keep an organized flight deck, use automation sensibly, tell ATC or your instructor what is happening, and transfer control clearly (ACS IR.IV.B.S2).
skills.practice: Before each session, brief control transfer and roles with your instructor [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]. In scenario flights, practice a recovery followed by a short call to ATC about the altitude deviation [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

quiz.q: During your cross-check, the VSI shows a climb rate that doesn't fit the maneuver you're flying. What does the IFH say to do?
options: Wait a few seconds to see if it settles
Trust the attitude indicator and ignore the VSI
Assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check
Engage the autopilot right away
quiz.why: Any rate or indication that doesn't fit the maneuver means assume an unusual attitude and increase the speed of the cross-check to confirm attitude, instrument error or failure [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

quiz.q: Nose-high with airspeed decreasing. What is your first control action by the IFH sequence?
options: Increase power
Level the wings
Pull back to stop the climb
Reduce power
quiz.why: Increase power, apply forward elevator, then level the wings. The inputs are almost simultaneous but in that order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

quiz.q: Nose-low with airspeed increasing. Which IFH sequence is correct?
options: Raise the nose, level the wings, reduce power
Reduce power, level the wings, raise the nose
Level the wings, add power, raise the nose
Reduce power, raise the nose, level the wings
quiz.why: Reduce power, correct bank with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Pulling with bank on only steepens the bank [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

quiz.q: On partial panel, what tells you the nose is passing through level pitch?
options: The turn coordinator's miniature aircraft levels
The ball centers
The heading stops changing
The airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse
quiz.why: When the airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse direction, the airplane is passing through level flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: Which of these is an upset by the AFH definition?
options: 20° nose up, 30° bank
8° nose down, 40° bank
15° nose up, 50° bank
5° nose down, 30° bank, cruise speed
quiz.why: Bank greater than 45° is an upset. The others stay under 25° nose up, 10° nose down and 45° bank at normal speed [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

quiz.q: In a long turn in IMC you feel wings level but see altitude dropping. What does the graveyard spiral tempt you to do?
options: Pull back, which tightens the spiral
Roll into a steeper bank
Push the nose down
Lean in your seat
quiz.why: The pilot feels a wings-level descent and pulls back, tightening the spiral and losing more altitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

quiz.q: On the IFH example PFD, what do the red chevrons on the attitude display point to?
options: The direction of the nearest airport
Back toward the horizon and level pitch
The direction of the turn
The flight director command bars
quiz.why: The red chevrons point back to the level pitch attitude. Pointing down means nose-high [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

quiz.q: In a spiral dive, after reducing power, what does the AFH say to do before rolling the wings level?
options: Pull firmly to stop the descent
Add full rudder against the turn
Lower the flaps to slow down
Apply some forward elevator to unload to about +1 G
quiz.why: A small forward push unloads the wing, reduces AOA and G-load and prevents a rolling pullout [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

quiz.q: A VFR pilot is in cloud and needs to turn. What is the AFH bank limit?
options: Standard rate, about 15°
Up to 30°
No more than 10°
Whatever brings the heading around fastest
quiz.why: Use the smallest practical bank, never more than 10°, turning in steps if needed [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

takeaways: Odd rate or reading on any instrument? Assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check.
Airspeed decides: slowing is nose high, speeding up is nose low.
Nose high: power up, push, roll. Nose low: power down, roll, then gently raise the nose.
No good attitude indicator? Recover on airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator; level pitch is when the needles stop and reverse.
Trust the instruments over your body. Illusions and startle push you the wrong way.
Disconnect automation to recover; use it afterward to cut workload.
Inadvertent IMC: wings level, gentle inputs (10° bank, 500 fpm), and ask for help early.
cfi_notes: The IFH nose-low order is power, bank, pitch [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The newer AFH spiral dive procedure adds a small forward push to about +1 G before rolling [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Teach the IFH order for the checkride and the unload for steep, high-G spirals; they don't conflict.

The AFH upset recovery template (Figure 5-3) is a graphic with no text in the handbook [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]. Show the figure in the printed AFH; this lesson teaches the procedure from the IFH and AFH text.

The IFH describes spillable gyros and caging [[23:114|IFH 5-19]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Most training airplanes today have nonspillable or electronic attitude displays. Teach that even a good one can be off up to 5° and hard to read in extreme attitudes.

The IFH glass panel numbers (chevrons at 30° and 15°, declutter at 65° bank, no standby turn coordinator) describe one example system [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Have the student find the same items in the POH supplement for their own avionics.
Common student error: fixing pitch first in a nose-low turn. Watch for the pull on the yoke before the wings are level, and have them call "power, roll, pull" out loud.

In unusual attitude training the pilot is often told to close their eyes, which removes surprise [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Add surprise in training, such as covering an instrument or failing the vacuum mid-scenario, because real upsets come with startle [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Clear the area above and below before every setup, and remind safety pilots that they tend to look inside during simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].
Keep demonstrations inside 60° bank and 30° pitch if anyone other than crew is aboard, unless everyone wears a parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].
gaps: The ACS gives no numeric tolerance for IR.IV.B.S1; the sources describe sequence and technique only.

Airplane-specific recovery steps, including configuration items such as flaps or gear, come from the POH/AFM, which is not in these sources. The AFH stall recovery mentions speedbrakes and spoilers only.
The AFH Figure 5-3 upset recovery template and Figure 5-18 spiral dive template are graphics whose text could not be read from the source.

For K3, the sources give AFH emergency control techniques and AIM assistance procedures, but no FAA procedure for a 180° turn out of IMC or for requesting an IFR clearance after inadvertent IMC as an instrument-rated pilot.
Avionics-specific unusual attitude protection and autopilot behavior (other than the IFH example system) are not covered.

activities.title: Illusion and the wrong reaction
activities.intro: Tap an illusion, then what the disoriented pilot tends to do.

pairs.r: Pulls back and tightens the descending turn
Rolls back into the original bank
Senses rotation on a different axis after a head movement
Feels nose-up while accelerating and pushes into a dive
Feels tumbling backward after leveling off
Chases a stationary light that seems to move

activities.title: Nose-high or nose-low?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Sound of rising speed in a steep turn
PFD red chevrons pointing down toward the horizon
First IFH recovery step: reduce power
First IFH recovery step: increase power

activities.title: Recover from a nose-low unusual attitude
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Notice the odd rate and speed up the cross-check
Level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder
Raise the nose with smooth back pressure
Cross-check for overcontrol until the needles stop and reverse
Bring the attitude indicator back into the cross-check

activities.title: True or false: failures, limits and inadvertent IMC
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the IFH example glass airplane, an AHRS failure removes all unusual attitude protection.
cards.why: Yes. The AHRS failure also removes attitude and heading from the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

cards.s: A VFR pilot who enters cloud should use about 30° of bank to turn back quickly.
cards.why: No. Use the smallest practical bank, never more than 10° [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

cards.s: A pilot without instrument training typically loses control within about 10 minutes on instruments alone.
cards.why: Yes, per accident statistics, for untrained pilots or those with eroded skills [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

cards.s: Below maneuvering speed, full control inputs in two axes at once cannot damage the airplane.
cards.why: No. Flying at or below VA doesn't protect against full inputs in more than one axis at the same time [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

cards.s: VNE is safe in rough air because it is set for all conditions.
cards.why: No. Never-exceed dive speeds are set for smooth air only. In rough air slow to maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

cards.s: The AIM says you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you become doubtful about the weather.
cards.why: Yes. That is the time to ask for help, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC your attitude indicator shows wings level, but the turn coordinator shows a left turn, the VSI shows a descent, the altimeter is unwinding, airspeed is rising and the suction gauge reads low. What is the best action?
options: Trust the attitude indicator and hold what it shows
Recover from a nose-low left turn using airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator
Pull back to stop the descent, then check the turn coordinator
Engage the autopilot so it can follow the attitude indicator
final_quiz.why: An attitude indicator that disagrees with the other instruments and a low suction reading point to a vacuum failure [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. Recover using the airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. An autopilot fed by wandering gyros can move wrongly [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots wings level. You pull 2 G while recovering from a dive. About what is the stall speed now?
options: 50 knots
60 knots
71 knots
100 knots
final_quiz.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: 50 × √2 ≈ 71 knots [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. 100 knots would take 4 G.

final_quiz.q: In a steep spiral you're banked about 80°. If you tried to hold altitude by pulling, about what load factor would you need, and how does that compare to a normal category airplane's limit?
options: About 2 G, below the limit
About 3.8 G, right at the limit
About 4.4 G, at the utility limit
About 5.76 G, well above the 3.8 G limit
final_quiz.why: A level 80° bank takes 5.76 G; the normal category limit is 3.8 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. That is why you roll wings level before you pull [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: After a recovery you're stable but 300 ft below your assigned altitude. Using the IFH rule of thumb, what climb rate do you use to return?
options: About 600 fpm, if within the airplane's optimum climb rate
About 300 fpm
Full power and best rate, whatever that gives
About 150 fpm
final_quiz.why: Use a vertical speed about double the altitude deviation, but never more than the optimum rate for the airplane: 2 × 300 = 600 fpm [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

final_quiz.q: On a dark night you go around and add full power quickly in IMC. You suddenly feel a steep nose-up pitch. What is the danger?
options: The inversion illusion makes you climb more
The somatogravic illusion tempts you to push into a nose-low or dive attitude
The leans make you roll into a bank
Autokinesis makes the runway lights seem to move
final_quiz.why: Rapid acceleration creates the somatogravic illusion of nose-up. The disoriented pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your autopilot starts a slow, uncommanded roll and you are already at 50° of bank. What should you do first?
options: Try a different autopilot mode
Reduce power and wait for the autopilot to recover
Disconnect the autopilot and fly the recovery by hand
Pull back to hold altitude while you troubleshoot
final_quiz.why: Disengaging the autopilot lets you control the airplane directly and may remove the cause [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Failing to disconnect is a common recovery error [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH example glass airplane, both the AHRS and the air data computer fail in IMC. What does the manufacturer recommend?
options: Turn on the autopilot, which works as a wing leveler
Fly the magnetic compass and VSI tape only
Use the standby turn coordinator
Reset the PFD by pulling its circuit breaker
final_quiz.why: With AHRS and ADC failed there is no attitude on the PFD, and the manufacturer recommends turning on the autopilot, simply a wing leveler. This airplane has no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

final_quiz.q: Why can't you fully trust a working nonspillable attitude indicator in an extreme attitude?
options: It always tumbles past 30° of bank
It reads only bank, not pitch
It shows a mirror image in steep attitudes
It can be off by up to 5° and is very hard to read
final_quiz.why: Even a working nonspillable instrument may have errors up to 5° of pitch and bank and is very difficult to interpret in extreme attitudes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

final_quiz.q: You are a VFR pilot who has slipped into cloud. ATC is giving rapid heading and altitude changes and you feel rushed. What does the AFH advise?
options: Do each change as fast as you can to please the controller
Ask the controller to slow down rather than rush a maneuver
Stop talking to ATC until you are in the clear
Combine the turn and the descent to save time
final_quiz.why: Don't let a sense of urgency rush you into a maneuver that could cost control; it's reasonable to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]. Combined maneuvers should be avoided [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

final_quiz.q: You want to practice unusual attitudes under a hood with a friend. What does 14 CFR 91.109(c) require of the safety pilot?
options: Only that they hold a student pilot certificate
An instrument rating and a current medical
A flight instructor certificate
At least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class, and adequate outside vision
final_quiz.why: The other control seat must hold a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate with appropriate category and class ratings, with adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your instructor puts you in a 30° bank with the nose 15° up while your eyes are closed. How does the AFH classify this?
options: An unusual attitude, but not an upset
An upset, because the bank is over 25°
A stall, because the nose is high
A spiral dive
final_quiz.why: The AFH uses this exact example: it is an unusual attitude but doesn't meet the upset parameters (over 25° nose up, over 10° nose down, over 45° bank) [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot in an upset doesn't realize anything is wrong and takes no corrective action. Which type of spatial disorientation is this?
options: Recognized
Unrecognized
Incapacitating
Vestibular overload
final_quiz.why: Unrecognized spatial disorientation: the pilot is unaware an upset is developing or has occurred and takes no corrective action [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC at night you are nose-low in a steep left bank with airspeed building. Which reaction does the IFH warn is instinctive and wrong?
options: Reducing power
Leveling the wings with the turn coordinator
Pulling back on the elevator first
Centering the ball
final_quiz.why: The instinctive reaction to a nose-down attitude is to pull back [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. With bank on, elevator alone steepens the bank and stresses the airplane [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
